extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and general readers of English drama and Ben Jonson
extracted.subtask_description: Critical-introduction style guidance on evaluating and understanding Ben Jonson's plays (theory, technique, and historical practice), especially his comedies, masques, and tragedies. Emphasises dramaturgical principles such as the comedy of humours, satire, construction, classical learning, and stagecraft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy of humours (characters conceived on a ruling trait)
rubrics_metrics.description: A humour, according to Jonson, was a bias of disposition, a warp, 'Some one peculiar quality / Doth so possess a man, that it doth draw / All his affects, his spirits, and his powers, / In their confluctions, all to run one way.' Jonson's comedy of humours conceived of stage personages on the basis of a ruling trait or passion, and by placing these typified traits in juxtaposition in their conflict and contrast, struck the spark of comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create characters dominated by a single ruling trait that governs their behaviour; dramatise comedy by juxtaposing such types. Anti-pattern: do not degrade a 'humour' into mere affectation (e.g., a bird wearing a pied feather) or reduce it to an oddity of dress, speech, or a fashion accessory — Jonson warns that that is 'more than most ridiculous.' Examples: Downright the plain squire; Bobadill the braggart-coward; Brainworm the professional fool.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classical learning and restraint (classicist ideals)
rubrics_metrics.description: Jonson was a classicist who 'believed in restraint and precedent in art' and held that a professional way of doing things might be reached by a study of the best examples among the ancients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value disciplined imitation and study of classical models to shape form, taste, and moral purpose. At the same time, Jonson does not insist on slavish adherence to every classical formalism — he allows licence comparable to the ancients and rejects those who would force 'strict and regular forms' in a way that is mere 'form.' Use classical authorities to inform design without losing dramatic freedom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional craftsmanship versus amateurishness
rubrics_metrics.description: Jonson objected to the amateurishness and haphazard nature of many contemporary plays and set himself to do something different — to practise a professional way of making drama.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasise studied composition, technical care, and learned craft in plotting, characterization, and language rather than loose, episodic, or slapdash construction. The criterion rewards conscious technique and control over mere spontaneity or undisciplined invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satire: righteous indignation, vivid caricature, and twofold attack
rubrics_metrics.description: Jonson's comical satires contain two kinds of attack: the generally satiric (critical) levelled at abuses and corruptions, and the personal in which specific contemporaries are lampooned; true satire must proceed 'by that righteous indignation which must lie at the heart of all true satire.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective satire combines principled moral purpose with sharp caricature. Be conscious of consequences: personal lampooning is an established dramatic practice but risks real quarrels and reprisals. Use satire to illuminate abuses or pretension, but be aware of the ethical and social costs of direct personal caricature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vivid characterisation grounded in observation of contemporary life
rubrics_metrics.description: Jonson's success rests on plays 'admirably written and each character is vividly conceived, and with a firm touch based on observation of the men of the London of the day.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Base comic types and individual characters on careful observation of social manners, professions, and city life to achieve vividness and verisimilitude. Specificity of detail and familiarity with contemporary London manners strengthen characterization (analogy made to Dickens as a recorder of his city).

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural ingenuity: central conceit, construction, and escalating climax
rubrics_metrics.description: Jonson's comedies often hinge on a central device or conceit (e.g., The Silent Woman: 'the whole comedy hinges on a huge joke') and exhibit construction in which 'the whole fabric building climax on climax' (example: The Alchemist).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design plays around a strong central idea or conceit and construct scenes so that complications accumulate plausibly toward successive climaxes. Balance ingenious contrivance with enough plausibility so the audience suspends disbelief; beware of departures from life's possibilities that undermine credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form and style choices (use of prose for comedy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Jonson wrote some comedies in prose (e.g., Every Man in His Humour), a practice modeled by John Lyly and notable in his technique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select verse or prose deliberately to suit comic aims. Prose can serve comedy effectively (dialogue-driven satire, realist scenes); be aware of precedents and their effects on tone and audience expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scholarly research and authoritative sourcing for historical drama
rubrics_metrics.description: In works like Sejanus Jonson read Tacitus, Suetonius, and other authorities 'to be certain of his facts, his setting, and his atmosphere,' even noting his authorities in the margin when printed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For historical or classical subjects, conduct careful research in source materials to ensure accuracy of fact, setting, and atmosphere; such scholarship increases authenticity even at the cost of occasional pedantry. Use classical sources to inform rhetoric, speech patterns, and historical detail (Jonson even modeled speeches on Cicero).

rubrics_metrics.name: Masque innovation and integration of spectacle (antimasque and stagecraft)
rubrics_metrics.description: Jonson gave dramatic value to the masque, especially by inventing the antimasque (a comic/farcical element for relief, entrusted to professional players or dancers) and by collaborating with Inigo Jones on mechanical and scenic invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design courtly entertainments and spectacle so that dramatic elements (antimasque, dances, costuming, scenic machinery) enhance rather than merely decorate the performance; integrate choreography and visual design with poetic and rhetorical aims. Collaboration with designers/architects can raise standards of stage representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral purpose and social critique balanced with comic method
rubrics_metrics.description: Jonson (like Dickens in Ward's comparison) is described as a moralist seeking truth by the exaggerated methods of humour and caricature; his work combines satire with pathos and a 'largeness of heart.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for moral or social insight beneath comic surface: satire and caricature should illuminate human folly and ideally contribute to a corrective or ethical impression. Preserve humane feeling and pathos alongside ridicule so the work 'leaves the world better for the art.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance between caricature and realism; avoid Rabelaisian excess
rubrics_metrics.description: Jonson's humour is 'always open to this danger' of loosening into Rabelaisian mode (as in Bartholomew Fair), where caricature may become excessive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain a balance: caricature and grotesque comedy are effective but must be reined so they do not collapse into merely coarse or excessive buffoonery. Keep satirical purpose and proportion to avoid alienating readers/viewers or undermining underlying critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial revision, collected edition practice, and textual care
rubrics_metrics.description: Jonson's 1616 collected edition published plays, poetry, and masques 'in a carefully revised text' — an unusual and significant act of authorial control at the time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice careful revision and consider collected publication as a way to present a controlled, authoritative text. Revision and annotation (e.g., noting authorities) reflect an author's intention and can guide readers and performers toward a more faithful understanding of the work.
